topics: 🏁 A Priest's Own Dedicated Field — why he can't simply keep it at the Jubilee
🤔 The Kal Vaḥomer That Almost Worked — 'I inherit others' fields, why not my own entirely?'
🎁 Rami bar Ḥama's Rejected Theory — comparing a dedicated field to a priest's sacrificial portions
🏞️ Rav Naḥman's Accepted Distinction — 'his ancestral field' stays with him; 'his dedicated field' does not
🎓 The Tractate Concludes — Masechet Arakhin ends on this final verse

overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Final Sugya of Masechet Arakhin
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 34a
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The tractate's very last sugya returns to a single phrase from Leviticus 27:21 and asks why it was necessary at all. A priest who received a dedicated field and then consecrated it himself might reason that since he already keeps a share of fields dedicated by others when the Jubilee arrives, he should certainly keep his own field entirely. The Gemara tests two different explanations for why the Torah needed to block this reasoning explicitly, rejecting one and accepting the other, before the daf — and with it, all of Arakhin — comes to a close.

slides.title: 🏁 The Baraita's Core Teaching
slides.subtitle: A priest cannot claim his own dedicated field, even though he shares in others'
rows: An Israelite consecrates his ancestral field, never redeems it, Jubilee arrives
Field is divided among ALL priests of the currently serving watch
The standard rule (established earlier in the tractate)
A priest receives a dedicated (ḥerem) field from someone else, THEN consecrates it himself, never redeems it
Field is likewise divided among his priestly brethren — NOT kept by him alone
Derived by juxtaposing 'his dedicated field' to an ordinary Israelite's ancestral field
'I already acquire a share of fields dedicated by OTHERS — surely I keep my OWN entirely!'

slides.title: 🤔 Testing the Priest's Kal Vaḥomer
slides.subtitle: Is the a fortiori argument even a fair comparison?

lines.speaker: The priest's claim
lines.text: If I acquire a share of fields that OTHER people consecrated and left unredeemed, then with regard to a field that is entirely MY OWN, shouldn't I certainly keep it?

lines.speaker: Gemara's first objection
lines.text: But these cases aren't equivalent! With others' fields, you merely acquire ONE share among many priestly brothers. Here, you'd be claiming the WHOLE field for yourself alone — a much bigger claim needing its own justification.

lines.speaker: Rami bar Ḥama
lines.text: Still, the verse is needed — you might otherwise think a dedicated field counts as 'his hallowed things' (Num. 5:10), which a priest may keep entirely.

lines.speaker: Rejection
lines.text: Not comparable: a priest's sacrificial portions were never truly 'in his possession' to begin with — he receives them as compensation from the Temple altar. Here, the field genuinely sits in the priest's own hands.

slides.title: 🎁 Rami bar Ḥama's Theory, and Why It Falls Short
slides.subtitle: An attempt to justify the verse's necessity

steps.content: 1️⃣ Question: why would I think a priest could keep his own dedicated field entirely?
2️⃣ Numbers 5:10: 'every man's hallowed things shall be his' — a priest keeps the priestly portions of offerings he personally sacrifices
3️⃣ Maybe a dedicated field, too, counts as his own 'hallowed thing' once it's in his hands?
4️⃣ Rejected: sacrificial portions are compensation 'from the table of the Most High' — never truly his to begin with. A field he actually possesses is a fundamentally different case

slides.title: 🏞️ Rav Naḥman's Distinction: The One That Sticks
slides.subtitle: 'His ancestral field' vs. 'his dedicated field' — two different Hebrew words, two different outcomes

nodes.content: ❓ Why might I think a priest's dedicated field is protected like his own inherited land?
💭 Leviticus 25:34: a Levite/priest's own ancestral field is 'their perpetual possession' — always redeemable, always returns to him
🔗 Perhaps the SAME protection extends to a field dedicated to him by someone else, once it's his?

✅ Accepted distinction: the verse's own wording separates them — 'his ACHUZATO' (his inherited ancestral field) stays with him forever; 'his ḤERMO' (his dedicated field) does NOT — it is divided among his priestly brethren at the Jubilee

slides.title: 🎓 The Tractate Concludes
slides.subtitle: Arakhin's final words
slides.label: Hadran — 'We shall return to you':
slides.text: With this sugya, Masechet Arakhin comes to its close. The tractate opened with who is included in the laws of valuations, moved through vows of assessment, the wealth-scaled valuations of Hesseg Yad, weight- and height-vows, dedications (ḥerem), and the intricate laws of redeeming fields, walled-city houses, and courtyard houses at or near the Jubilee — ending, fittingly, on a final fine distinction about what a priest may and may not keep for himself.
slides.hebrewSource: הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ הַמּוֹכֵר שָׂדֵהוּ, וּסְלִיקָא לָהּ מַסֶּכֶת עֲרָכִין

summary.principle: Even a priest who personally received and then consecrated a dedicated field cannot claim it entirely for himself at the Jubilee — the Torah's own wording distinguishes his truly inherited ancestral field, which stays with him forever, from a field merely dedicated to him, which is divided among his priestly brethren like any other.

flowSteps.content: 🏁 A priest's own dedicated field, if consecrated and unredeemed, is divided among all priests — not kept by him alone
🤔 His tempting kal vaḥomer ('I share in others' fields, so surely I keep my own') fails — the cases aren't truly parallel

columns.content: 🎁 Rami bar Ḥama's theory (sacrificial portions) rejected — those were never really his to begin with
🏞️ Rav Naḥman's distinction accepted — 'his ancestral field' vs. 'his dedicated field' are simply different

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Masechet Arakhin concludes: valuations, vows, dedications, and field-redemption laws, closing on this final precise distinction

quiz.q: According to the baraita, what happens to a field that a PRIEST himself received as a dedication (ḥerem) and then consecrated, if it remains unredeemed at the Jubilee?
o: The priest keeps the entire field for himself
It is divided among all the priests of the currently serving watch, just like an ordinary Israelite's unredeemed ancestral field
It automatically reverts to the original donor
It becomes property of the Levites instead of the priests
quiz.e: The baraita teaches that even though a priest already holds this field as his own dedicated property, it is still divided among his priestly brethren at the Jubilee — he may not claim it entirely for himself.

quiz.q: What is the priest's kal vaḥomer (a fortiori) argument for why he should be allowed to keep his own dedicated field, and why does the Gemara initially question whether this comparison is even valid?
o: He argues the field is worthless; the Gemara agrees it's a fair comparison

He argues that since he already acquires a SHARE of fields dedicated by others, he should keep his OWN field entirely — but the Gemara notes acquiring one share among many priests is not comparable to claiming an entire field alone
He argues that priests never lose any property; the comparison is deemed perfectly valid
He cites a completely different verse about tithes
quiz.e: The priest reasons that since he shares in fields dedicated by others (albeit only a fractional share, as one of many priestly brothers), he should certainly keep his own field, which is entirely in his possession — a much larger claim that the Gemara initially questions as not truly parallel.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara reject Rami bar Ḥama's suggestion that a priest's dedicated field should be compared to 'his hallowed things' (Numbers 5:10), which a priest may keep for himself?
o: Because that verse doesn't exist
Because a priest's sacrificial portions were never actually 'in his possession' to begin with — he receives them as compensation, unlike a field he genuinely holds
Because dedicated fields are never actually owned by anyone
Because the comparison was accepted, not rejected
quiz.e: The Gemara distinguishes: a priest's portions from offerings he sacrifices are compensation he receives 'from the table of the Most High,' never truly his personal possession beforehand — while a dedicated field genuinely sits in his own hands, making the comparison invalid.

quiz.q: According to Rav Naḥman's accepted resolution, what is the key textual distinction that explains why a priest's OWN INHERITED ancestral field stays with him forever, but his DEDICATED field does not?
o: There is no distinction; both are treated identically

The verse's own wording distinguishes 'his ancestral field' (achuzato), which remains his perpetual possession, from 'his dedicated field' (ḥermo), which is divided among his priestly brethren at the Jubilee
The distinction is based purely on the field's monetary value
The distinction depends on which tribe originally owned the field
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman explains that the verse's precise language separates a priest's genuinely inherited ancestral field (achuzato), protected as perpetual possession, from a field merely dedicated to him by someone else (ḥermo), which does not receive that same protection.

quiz.q: What Hebrew phrase marks the conclusion of Masechet Arakhin at the end of this daf, and what does it mean?
o: 'Baruch Hashem' — a simple blessing with no special significance
'Hadran alach' ('we shall return to you') followed by 'u'slika lah Masechet Arakhin' ('and thus concludes Tractate Arakhin')
'Ein od milvado' — an unrelated theological statement
There is no closing formula; the daf simply stops mid-discussion
quiz.e: The daf closes with the traditional formula 'Hadran alach ha-mokher sadeihu, u'slika lah Masechet Arakhin' — 'we shall return to you, [the chapter] "One who sold his field," and thus concludes Tractate Arakhin' — marking the formal end of the tractate.
